Chibíkumọnai 1 Wòmíseiró Waters’ Rest: the flooding ends and leaves fertile land. Chibíkumọnai 20 Zhawézónímís The Death and Life Festival. Young Anu complete their recitation of the thirty threads before it. Chibíkumọnai 30 Rạdíkhèti The Longest Light, the summer solstice festival. Lòbárạdímọnai 14 Rạdí‘ówáné The Sun Festival. Mbòmọnai 30 Égékhèm’ärạmís Sacred Eternal Mother Day. Nèbémọnai 1 Kwómüyí First cold. The second school term begins. Khósúmọnai 1 Naudùyítánéka Balance of the Dark, the autumn equinox festival. Khósúmọnai 16 to 18 Fómíka’ówáné The Harvest Festival. Khósúmọnai 30 Khùmówáné The Moon Festival. Wòtómọnai 10 to 16 Tikhètùbẹsé The Great Shifting: a week of heightened connection to animal spirits and stronger transformation. Rábímọnai 15 Bízháwạmís Love and Family Day. Rábímọnai 30 Khùmikhèti The Longest Night, the winter solstice festival. Kwọnákhạmọnai 1 Rïkhákhètímís The Grand Rebirth: an end-of-year rite when many acolytes are initiated. The thirteenth sign of the year, Daimùtèzun the Dreamwalker, belongs to the sacred days. See The 13 Signs . Name days The first and senior Sekh clan is honoured by name in the way a saint is. Each member’s day is their Initiation Day, and many Nok families choose their children’s names from them. Amadi’s own name is not used, although many names are inspired by it. The list itself is kept in the private canon. Drift The equinox and solstice festivals have drifted over time from their astronomical dates. Khùmäyítánéka, for example, now falls on Mar 6 rather than near Mar 20. Decided Friday’s name, Háshùdíma, follows the settled spelling of Háshùmün, and Thursday’s name, Hóshédíma, follows its god Hóshémün the same way. Decided

h: Timeline How the city began Hurste, on the eastern bank Emerson, on the western bank Who runs the city The five human families The Witches of Mephis in Emsehurst Places Where it is What the city says about itself Peoples of the city Ordinary humans
x: Home / Earth / Emsehurst Emsehurst A river city that belongs to more than one kind of living thing. It began as two towns facing each other across the Squannock River. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. A tourist’s guide map of Emsehurst. Illustrated, not to scale. Timeline Year Event 1725 Hurste is founded by migrating Sekh and their human Zingan followers, seeking isolation and freedom from outside government. 1738 Yírímbo Zonémi is established in Hurste. 1805 Emerson is founded by a settler caravan north of the Emmers River, in what is now the Historical District. About 1808 to 1810 The Emerson catastrophe and the founding witch contracts. 1924 Emerson and Hurste are incorporated as one municipality, Emsehurst. 1933 The original Pandora’s Pact is signed. 1964 The Lamiae are admitted through the Pact addendum. 1968 The interstate is completed, speeding trade, commuting and mixing between the old communities. The two towns were never cut off from each other. Roads, trade and above all the ferries of the Porters District joined them long before the interstate. Incorporation in 1924 did not erase the old divisions of culture, housing and money. Decided How the city began Hurste, on the eastern bank Hurste began in what is now the Zingan Quarter, around Moreau College and the Temple, and spread north. Its founders were Sekh and the human Zingans who followed them, looking for a place where no government would reach them. Decided Many Quaker families settled there later. Their belief in the Inner Light and practical tolerance let them live quietly beside things other settlers fled or burned. Indigenous communities lived in the surrounding country before either town existed. Relations with Hurste were mostly cordial, with trade, truces, understandings and some intermarriage. When forced removal and persecution drove people from their lands, many sought shelter in Hurste. Some joined its population without taking up the Sekhmetian faith. This almanac keeps those peoples and that history deliberately general. Decided Emerson, on the western bank In 1805 a settler caravan stopped north of the Emmers River and founded Emerson. Eight families led it: Emmers, Bonchild, Gilbert, Somerhalder, Payne, Malcolm, Jacobsen and Deschamps. Decided For a few years the town prospered. Then people began to vanish in the dark hours, even after curfews and a militia. The Jacobsen and Deschamps families were attacked and destroyed, and some of their members may have been Turned into Lamiae. The Malcolm family fled. John Emmers, the settlement’s leader, was taken. Settlers returned from the dark with something else behind their eyes, and the fear that followed ended with a surviving teenager burned at the stake. Prayers went unanswered. What came was a visitor who called himself Itzal, one of many names he has used over the centuries. He offered five of the town’s families a compact: power to protect the settlement in exchange for a lasting bond. Emmers, Bonchild, Gilbert, Somerhalder and Payne signed. They became the local witch families, and Emerson survived. The Witches of Mephis already existed elsewhere. These five did not found the network. They built its power structure in this city. Decided In 1924 Emerson and Hurste became the city of Emsehurst. The Quaker families of both towns found each other and formed one Meeting, and have been a quiet, knowing presence ever since. Who runs the city Emsehurst is run through ordinary municipal government, long dominated by the five witch families. The Emmers family is its leading political dynasty, as long-lived and prominent as the Kennedys. Many Emmers have been mayor. They are usually non-magical relatives, who are less likely to fall to the madness that witchcraft can bring. Most know something of the supernatural world, though how much varies. The family’s civic power and its supernatural power overlap without always sitting in the same person. The Pact, informal agreements and backroom deals run alongside the council chamber. Decided The five human families The Quaker Meeting is five families of different ages and origins, and the arrangement has held for about two centuries. They share a theology of tolerance and an inherited understanding of what the city is. They do not talk about it. They ask few questions of their supernatural neighbours, have never taken anything from them and have never been taken from. Family Came from Wealth Mercer Emerson settlers Banking. The Bank of Emsehurst, formerly the First Bank of Emerson. The city’s main bank since before it was incorporated. Waller Emerson settlers Land and property. Some of the oldest deeds in the city carry the name. Langford Hurste founding stock Civic and property wealth. Builders of schools and halls, more interested in building institutions than owning them. Porter Hurste founding stock Trade and shipping, through the Porter Trading Company. The Porters district bears the name. Colby Arrived after incorporation Established city business interests. The newest of the five. The Witches of Mephis in Emsehurst The Witches of Mephis hold blood contracts with the being the city knew as Itzal, whom witches call Mephis. Each contract carries a price personal to the signer, and each must be renewed every ten generations. The network is global and about two thousand years old. Emsehurst is its showcase chapter, and the most sophisticated the patron has built. The whole story is in The Witches of Mephis . Family Standing in the city Emmers The most politically prominent. The city’s leading dynasty, with many mayors, usually non-magical relatives. Payne A foundational family with strong ties to magical practice and to mediation between factions. Gilbert The most publicly visible, running Crossroads Apothecary. Now in the tenth generation and facing the question of renewal. Bonchild Lower public profile than the Emmers or Gilberts but deeply embedded in the city’s supernatural working. A family member heads the Orbis Conservatory. Somerhalder Eliminated from Emsehurst by a Human Coalition raid in 1970, when the movement still went by the name Light of Humanity. The seat has been empty since. The five families signed together, in the order Emmers, Bonchild, Gilbert, Somerhalder, Payne. They are the Witches’ signatories to Pandora’s Pact . Five more lines joined the network later, each with its own origin. See the ten family lines . Places The Squannock River divides the old western and eastern towns. The Zingan Quarter and the Merveilles Valley lie east of it. Mixed territories are Money Street, the University of Emsehurst, the Zingan Quarter and the SxSW entertainment districts. Anu lands are the mountain and forest country east of the Squannock. See Pandora’s Pact . Where it is Emsehurst is a fictional city in the American Northeast, and its state is deliberately never named. It has river valleys, hills, bridges and an industrial past, like Western Pennsylvania and Ohio. To the east rise the Merveilles Mountains, the setting’s Appalachian country and home to the Anu. Chicago, New York and Philadelphia exist as places to travel to. About thirty minutes away lies Asheville, which in this world has a beach and ocean access. Decided What the city says about itself Emsehurst has the reputation of Salem or Forks. Its legends are familiar to everyone and part of the city’s identity. Some residents believe, some enjoy the stories, and others have never noticed, do not care, or scoff. The Human Coalition feeds this atmosphere, spreading conspiracy theories that blend real incidents with misinformation and invented threats. Decided Peoples of the city Pandora’s Pact The 1933 agreement and the 1964 Lamiae addendum. The Lamiae The vampires of the SxSW districts and signatories since 1964. The Witches of Mephis Blood contracts, ten family lines and the Consortium’s sixty schools. Zingans Human devotees of ’Èn’zíngámün, their quarter and their college. Human Coalition and Basilica The two organised human groups that oppose the supernatural world. Bediens and Servi Humans bound to Lamiae, from the addicted to the blood-bonded. Ordinary humans Humans have no supernatural abilities and the usual weaknesses: illness, injury, death. Sekh blood has a steroid-like effect when it is not used in the Rebirth rite. Lamiae blood is a euphoric, aphrodisiac and highly addictive drug. Both leave a heavy toll on the body once the first effects fade.

h: The five layers Level 1: the two foundations Level 2: the four pillars Level 3: the seven spirits of virtue Level 4: the twelve principles Level 5: the thirty threads How the threads are kept Strict communities
x: Home / Earth / Nẹránamün / Moral framework Moral framework Five layers of law, from two sentences carved on every gate to thirty daily threads. The Anu and the Sekh each have their own wording. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. The moral laws of Nẹránamün are universal to all children of the Dream. The Anu hold the thread tightly, as keepers of the border and guardians of the dead. The Sekh walk it boldly, with fire in their step. Humans honour the laws in breath and memory. The Anu proverb is “Words fade. The hunt endures.” The Sekh say, “What burns is alive. What endures is wise.” The old lists of 42 and 34 Confessions are retired, and the code stays at thirty threads. Decided The five layers Level Anu name Sekh name Where it lives 1 The 2 Foundations, the Twin Pillars of the Dream The 2 Foundations, the Twin Flames of Existence Carved in every Anu meeting place. On Sekh temple gates and clan seals. 2 The 4 Pillars, the Four Legs of the Hunt The 4 Pillars, the Four Claws of the Hunt Taught first to Anu children, alongside survival skills. Written in Sekh scrolls for children. 3 The 7 Spirits of Virtue, the Spirit Path The 7 Spirits of Virtue, the Fire Path Anu children aged 3 to 6. Marked on ceremonial weapons, talismans and clan engravings. 4 The 12 Cycle Principles, the Dreamers’ Oath The 12 Ember Oaths Anu children aged 7 to 10. Recited at councils, trials, gatherings and initiations. 5 The 30 Threads, the Threadkeepers’ Code The 30 Threads, Sekh Edition Anu children aged 11 to 15. Recited daily by devout Anu, devout Sekh and elder Zingans. Level 1: the two foundations Anu edition Sekh edition Honor the cycle of life and death. Honor the cycle of fire and ash. Protect the pack, protect the Dream. Protect the Pride, protect the thread. Level 2: the four pillars Anu edition Sekh edition Walk in the flow of Time, never against it. Walk in the rhythm of Time’s fire. Hunt with purpose, not for pride. Hunt with purpose, not for vanity. Keep the pack strong and whole. Keep the Pride whole and strong. Honor the spirits of the earth and sky. Honor the spirits of earth and sky. Level 3: the seven spirits of virtue Both peoples share the same seven, the spirits Nyámün gave to Mbòngómün. Each is a virtue and a patron. Spirit Patron The virtue Gorilla ‘Èng’gímün Strength: protect your kin. Canina Bùnumün Loyalty: stand by the pack. Leopard Dùmeimün Stealth: know when to strike and when to wait. Chimpanzee Wòmün Adaptability: change with the hunt. Lizard ‘Otukútámün Rebirth: shed what weighs you down. Lion Rómün Courage: face all battles with fire. Eagle Maizomün Sight: see beyond what lies before you. Level 4: the twelve principles Anu: the Dreamers’ Oath Sekh: the Ember Oaths Do not kill without purpose. Do not kill without fire in your purpose. Do not betray your pack or mate. Do not betray your lineage or mate. Do not steal from kin. Do not steal from your kin. Do not abandon the wounded. Do not abandon the wounded of your Pride. Do not lie to save yourself. Do not lie to save your own flame. Do not forsake your bondmate. Do not desecrate your bondmate. Do not consume what is cursed. Do not consume what is cursed by the flame. Do not bury truth in silence. Do not bury truth beneath ash. Do not strike down the defenseless. Do not strike down the defenseless. Do not ignore a soul in pain. Do not turn from a cry in the dark. Do not hoard what the pack needs. Do not hoard the fire meant for the Pride. Do not mock the spirits or the Dream. Do not mock the spirits or the Dream. Level 5: the thirty threads The strictest layer. The two editions share a shape and differ in wording. The Anu hold the border and the dead. The Sekh carry fire. The wording is final. Decided Thread Anu: Threadkeepers’ Code Sekh edition 1 I honor the living, and I guide the dead. I honor the fire of the living and the embers of the dead. 2 I protect the weak of my pack. I protect the weak of my Pride. 3 I take from the land only what the pack will use. I name no one’s guilt before I have faced my own in the mirror. 4 I speak truth, even in shadow. I speak truth, even when it scorches me. 5 I walk the Hunt with purpose. I walk my Hunt with purpose. 6 I shield the pups until they have met their spirits. I shield the young from ruin. 7 I name no packmate traitor until I have followed the trail myself. I learn from the ashes of my mistakes. 8 I care for the wounded before myself. I tend the wounded before I feed my pride. 9 I do not turn my jaws on the defenseless. I do not let the bloodlust choose my prey. 10 I do not turn away from the call. I do not turn away from the call of the Hunt. 11 I remember the faces of my ancestors. I remember the faces of my bloodline. 12 I respect the spirits of the Hunt. I respect the spirits of the Hunt and Dream. 13 I share my kill with my pack. I give the Pride more than I take from it. 14 I stand watch over the resting places of the dead. I do not defile the resting places of the dead. 15 I do not take cursed blood into my body. I do not drink the blood of the damned. 16 I answer the cry of the Dream. I answer the cry of the Dream Thread. 17 I do not leave a packmate to die alone, or unburied. I do not abandon the one I have named. 18 I challenge with honor. I challenge with honor, not arrogance. 19 I accept the cycle of time. I accept the cycle of fire and ash. 20 I do not mate in deceit. I do not mate in deceit. 21 I honor my Miyema, and I do not cut a thread in anger. I cherish the bond of my mate and my Pride. 22 I heal what I can, and mourn what I cannot. I atone in the open for what I have burned wrongly. 23 I do not invite corruption into the pack. I do not invite corruption into my flame. 24 I keep the border I was given, and cross no pack’s without word. I mark my hunt grounds with respect. 25 I do not leave prey to suffer needlessly. I do not leave prey to suffer needlessly. 26 I bear my scars with pride. I fall in the open, and I rise in the open. 27 I do not mistake the pack’s strength for my own. I do not hide from sun, moon, or flame. 28 I teach the pups the Threads, and I keep my own. I burn to be alive, and I build what will outlast me. 29 I face death with honor. I face death as I face life, with fire. 30 I do not forget my name or my pack. I do not forget my name, nor my flame. How the threads are kept Daily recitation. Morning and night, five threads per rotation. Five a day over a six-day Nok week covers all thirty, and a 30-day month holds five such weeks. After each, people ask themselves: “Have I done this today? Do I need to cleanse or confess?” Teaching. The foundations and pillars come from toddlerhood, with survival lessons. The seven spirits come through fables, animal symbols and chants. The twelve come through mnemonic songs and scenarios. The full thirty come through call-and-response each moon, scrollwork in Nok and Common, and dream-watching journals. The initiation challenge. A young Anu recites all thirty in order, explains twenty chosen at random, lives a test week judged by elder watchers, and passes a soul-mirror trial before a ’Anpésùmün priest. Breaking a thread. Repeated breaks that are never repented weaken, decay or turn the spirit. A soul that dies with too many has no Shadow Walker path and wanders. Breaking one before others without confessing stains the bloodline’s name. Strict communities Some Anu live in devout enclaves, comparable to Hasidic communities: self-contained, ritual-precise and strict. Non-mates touch little after age 12, courtship is supervised and includes a confession of purity, and the community keeps a spiritual quarantine after contact with Lamiae blood. Fasting, silent walks and moon-watching are common. Shame in such a community carries to the whole bloodline.

x: Home / Earth / Nẹránamün Nẹránamün The faith of the Dream. It began among the Nok-speaking peoples and is the faith of the Sekh, the Anu and the human clergy who serve them. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. Names of the faith Name Use Nẹránamün The everyday name. Neinyámurámayámün “Celestial Order of the Creator’s Balance.” Used in holy texts, temple engravings, priesthood rites and academic settings. Khùzí-Khùzuwạkùn “Path of Ebb and Flow,” after the twin moons. Daimùzónobuwạkùn, Daimùyùn’äfẹrí Names pointing to the Dream itself. Nyáránamün A further variant listed in the source notes. Followers Shùkíneirana , the True Dreamers. Daimùyùnä , anyone descended from a Nẹránamün culture, practising or not. Hányídaimùyùnä , the Lost Dreamers, who have left the faith. Some call themselves Kiwásómùna , the woken ones. Shùkízíngámùna , colloquially Shùkízímù, are the human devotees of ‘Èn’zíngámün. In English they are the Zingans . Decided Core ideas The Dream. Nyámün, the All-Creator, dreamed the world into being. The Daimùzónobu is the Dream-Life-Thread that runs through everything. The Thread. Each life is a thread. Death is a divergence of paths, not an end. Twin moons. Time’s twin faces, ‘Írubá (ebb) and ‘Írábùkh (flow), made two moons, Khùzú and Khùzí. They later crashed together into a single scarred moon, Khùm, in the event called Dímakhùm Daimùzónobu. On Earth this is a story carried over from Kanna and passed down for centuries, so it is an intentional distortion of the original moons. Decided Khùm still carries both legacies: waxing, it remembers Khùzí’s fire, and waning, it whispers Khùzú’s memory. If Khùm ever splits again, the thread will fray and the age of balance will end. Two worlds, one veil. ‘Ätozo is the living world and ‘Ätáru the afterlife. Nèbémün keeps the Veil between them, Kàtúngámün’s river carries souls across, and Wạdíyèmün the Serpent Guardian protects the crossing. The soul Part Meaning Zhaní The land-self, doppelganger spirit or ego. Expressed by the Khùzí. Zhané The aerial self, personality or id. Expressed by the Khùzú. Neirú The divine self and spiritual power. The goddess weighs this at the Divine Threshold. N’keiní The physical body. Thaibi The shadow and mortality. It passes to ‘Anpésùmün at death. Learn more The pantheon Nyámün, Time, the twins, the sky and sea, and the seven spirits. Moral framework From two foundations down to thirty threads, in Anu and Sekh editions. Sacred arts and symbols Makésho, Dreamleaf, the sigils, and the clergy orders. Inspiration Nẹránamün is a fully original tradition, inspired by Kemetic and Yoruba practice but entirely its own. This almanac uses only Nẹránamün names. Decided

h: Society In Emsehurst What hurts a Lamia How others see them Open questions
x: Home / Earth / The Lamiae / Society and weaknesses Society, weaknesses and relations No kingdom and no code. A hunger shared by thousands, a few old bonds, and a long list of things that can kill them. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Lamiae reference (v3). Tags mark anything less settled. Society Structure. There is no central leader. Hashaeqa is the nominal ruler and rarely pays attention, so the Lamiae organise themselves: everyone out for themselves, with gangs and claimed turf. Covens are loose, with little loyalty unless it is forced. The Sireline. Every Lamia is bound to Hashaeqa through their Sireline. A Sire can die with little consequence beyond some mental pain. Generations. Nearly all the first generation died. The turned generations just after them are rumoured dead or hidden, and every generation since has been weaker. Lamiae call the turned “imperfect,” because the human blood that made them is the weak point. Where they live. Underground economies: clubs, dealing, trafficking. Humans may spot a Lamia faster than a Sekh, but Lamiae pass in the underground, with contacts, makeup and glasses to blend in. Much of vampire folklore comes from them. Feeding from each other is no use, except for personal interest. Moral framework. None is shared. The Sekh and the Anu live by the five-level framework, and the Lamiae have none, which is part of why the Anu hunt rabid ones. Proposed In Emsehurst The 1964 addendum to Pandora’s Pact made the Lamiae a signatory with the same obligations as the other parties. The Pact protects every human in and around Emsehurst. Taking a person from among them by force breaches it, and that includes trafficking. The trafficking that Lamiae criminals do is done in breach of the Pact, not outside it. Decided SxSW is where the Lamiae and their Bediens are most visible. A servus is bound by something a Lamia does , not by feeding. If the master dies, by any cause, the servus dies. See Bediens and Servi . What hurts a Lamia Weakness Effect Sunlight The day belongs to the Vatrajarə, so the sun is the Lamiae’s enemy. Brief exposure burns, and prolonged exposure burns them to a crisp. They keep a strict night cycle. Protection charms exist, but must be worn at all times and wear out the longer they are in the sun. Flames Healing kicks in at first, but it is hungry for energy, so a large or well-fed fire can kill. Some charms protect against the elements. Aethmaale Holy steel, forged to kill the fallen and their children. It burns outward from the point of contact. Fatal to Lamiae. Sovoq Infernal steel. It can hurt a Lamia, but nowhere near as badly as Aethmaale: a wound that would kill from Aethmaale is survivable from Sovoq. Decided Kraethjarə The aura flare of a Vatrajarə, in Vatraxu Kraethjaro. Depending on the blast it can burn a Lamia to dust. Sekh blood Small amounts cause vomiting and unconsciousness, and large amounts kill. Recovery takes vomiting or bloodletting and fresh human blood. Starvation About a week, then madness, then a wizened husk. How others see them People Relation The Sekh Older than the Sekh and roughly equal in power. Lamiae blood is toxic to Sekh, and Sekh blood is toxic to Lamiae. Each has made weapons from it. The Anu The Anu hunt “reckless or rabid” Lamiae. A large amount of Lamiae blood sends an Anu into a berserker state for 12 hours to 3 days. Strict Anu enclaves keep a quarantine after contact. Humans Prey, Bediens and Servi. The Witches of Mephis Lamiae blood is needed for the stronger witch spells. Witches also supply fortifying spells to Bediens by contract. The Vatrajarə Their saliva makes the Vatrajarə ill. Their light and their steel are the Lamiae’s worst weaknesses. Hashaeqa Nominal ruler, and Sire of every Sireline. Open questions Whether the heart-stone of the Lamiae counts as a Raqal in the Aempaera sense Open How far Turned Lamiae lose or keep their human functions, which is unwritten except for the first generation Open

h: At a glance Origin Turning Blood and addiction Bodies Abilities Emblem Read next
x: Home / Earth / The Lamiae The Lamiae A Lamia in modern dress. Concept image. The vampires of the Sekh Universe: older than the Sekh, never as organised, and bound to a hunger that began with a curse. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Lamiae reference (v3). Tags mark anything less settled. At a glance Names Lamike (one) and Lamikehi (many) in both Vatrahu and Vatraxu. Ancient Greeks met them and called them Lamia and Lamiae, and the names are interchangeable. The Sekh say KauNamä’i in Nok. The Greek name gave the human world part of its idea of the vampire. Decided Age A Lamia stays the age they were when turned. Eyes Round pupils, like a human’s or an Anu’s, never the Sekh’s oval. Always in some shade of red. Blood A special type called A-e. Diet Human blood only, fresh from a living person. Animal blood makes them ill, and food makes them vomit. They have no digestive system. The first generation could eat ordinary food when young. See Origin. Heart A calcified heart that does not beat or circulate blood. The first generation were born with it. Turned Lamiae gain it during the Turning. Decided Lifespan Essentially immortal until killed or starved. On death they burn to ash or shrivel. Rule In name they answer to Hashaeqa. In practice there is no central leader. In Emsehurst Signatories to Pandora’s Pact since 1964. They are most visible in the SxSW districts. Origin The first Lamiae were born, not made: eight children of Hashaeqa. They are a species of their own, not four kinds of one species. Her other children, by other mothers, are separate peoples. See The four broods . Decided The first generation was born with hearts already calcified, yet at first they lived much like humans. They could eat ordinary food, breathe, stand sunlight and have children. Over time the body calcifies further. Blood becomes necessary, tolerance for sunlight falls and fertility ends. Living in a more human way can slow the change, but it ends in death all the same, not in escape. Nearly all of the first generation died in the war of the Fall. Decided Every Lamia since was made: a human turned by another Lamia, whose heart calcifies in the Turning. So there are two kinds, the born and the turned, and they stay physically distinct. Most of what follows on this page describes the Turned. The old title “eldest of the Verdoem races” stands. In the terms of the Aempaera they are Vatrajaħə, Vatrajaxo in Vatraxu. They are older than the Sekh and roughly their equal in power. Decided No dates are given. The order of events is what counts. Decided Turning Who can turn. Any Lamia more than a year old. Turned Lamiae cannot have children. The first generation could, early in life. How. The Lamia drinks from the person, feeds them Lamiae blood and deals a killing blow, such as a snapped neck. No consent and no ceremony are needed. The amount of blood is not precise. A human who dies with Lamiae blood in them turns on their own. The waking. In 24 to 48 hours the person wakes as a Lamia with intense bloodlust, or stays dead. The first week they are fairly uncontrollable. The cost. How a person died, and the state of mind they died in, shape lasting psychological damage. A victim of a brutal murder may develop a compulsion to recreate the trauma. After. A newly turned Lamia’s telepathy reaches only across a small room. Many find their own way. Those in covens often stay with their new kin. Blood and addiction To humans, Lamiae blood in small amounts is euphoric and an aphrodisiac, like a powerful party drug, and it is profoundly addictive. The toll afterward is heavy. This is what produces the addicted tier of Bediens . It is toxic to everyone but humans, and it is toxic to the Sekh. It is also an antidote to Sekh blood in humans and other supernatural beings. Lamiae saliva is an aphrodisiac for prey and makes feeding pleasurable. It sickens the Vatrajarə and ranges from mild to fatal for the Sekh. Their blood is a major amplifier of witch spells, and for the strongest it may be required. See Contracts and power . Bodies Breathing is optional, and most do it from reflex. Their skin is about twice as tough as a human’s. They are cold-blooded, like reptiles, and do not feel temperature or the elements unless magic reinforces them. Height and weight are frozen. Hair and nails return to the state they were in when the person was turned: a bald man never regrows hair, and long hair always grows back to its final length. They are stronger, but cannot show it without hurting themselves. The magic gives everyone the same strength whatever their build, so a weak teenager who throws a car breaks a bone doing it. Tattoos and piercings: holes close faster and ink fades faster. Anything from before the Turning stays. The spell preserves the body as it was. Lost limbs do not regrow, and impairments such as deafness or blindness may or may not heal. Anything lost as a Lamia can be reattached if it was not burned away. The tongue thickens and the taste buds die. The palate is centred on blood, and other food tastes awful. They can go about a week without blood, then comes madness, then a wizened husk. Abilities Ability What it does Turning After a Lamia’s first year. Senses, speed and strength All heightened, within the limit above. Telepathy Between Lamiae, strongest along your Sireline, the chain of vampires linking you to Hashaeqa. Those higher in your line can block those below. Range grows with age. Temptation Subliminal messages sent by telepathy, to humans and former humans only. Strength varies by individual. Healing A surface wound heals in minutes. They survive more fatal blows than the Sekh and can move a severed body to reattach the head within an hour. Emblem Emblem of the Lamiae. Read next Society, weaknesses and relations Covens and gangs, the Sireline, the Pact, what hurts a Lamia, and how the other peoples see them. The four broods The Lamiae and three other peoples born in the same years: Veskari, Shavari and Kharuvi.

h: Names Sayings
x: Home / Earth / The Nok The Nok The people and language of Nẹránamün’s home. Nok is the liturgical language of the faith, and its calendar and schools are used across the Earth realm. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. Names People who speak Nok name children after a common ancestor, a personal trait or achievement, a favourite god, or the name that matches the calendar day of birth. Each day of the first twelve months of the Name Calendar (Khínai’gbasídí) carries two or three names. The thirteenth month is sacred and has none. Calendar and festivals Thirteen months, the sacred Khèmọnai, the six-day week and the festival year. The 13 Dream-Tethered Signs Birth signs: animal, patron and the Fang and Feather aspects of each. Schools How a Nok child is educated, and the named academies. The thread tradition How Anu wear and share their threads through life. Sayings Nok Meaning Zhèmí dạkúmé shù wónírèt. Wisdom begins in wonder. Ng’kọmunù’íz dạzòmù zhèmí’ö’z kúmémé. To know oneself is the beginning of wisdom. Fùgạ shùkírèt kwowạkùn! Go the path of following! Fùgạ díyí khíkón! Go through the lighted road! Sai mbè. Until again. Kwotó A casual goodbye, shortened from kwowạkùn fùdótó. Nok is agglutinative. A Nok reference grammar is planned. Open

h: The Human Coalition Where it came from The Basilica Sacrae Flammae Abilities Emblems
x: Home / Earth / Emsehurst / Coalition and Basilica Human Coalition and Basilica Two organised human groups who oppose the supernatural world. One fights with words and the other with fire. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. The Human Coalition The Coalition presents itself as reasonable. It never admits the supernatural exists. It speaks of “dangerous fringe groups,” “predatory cults” and “threats to ordinary families,” and that language has worked very well. Where it came from People of Christ. A Reconstruction-era Christian group, inspired by the young Ku Klux Klan, which excluded non-white people for a long time. Decided Light of Humanity. Its successor: violent and badly organised. It carried out the 1970 raid. The Human Coalition. The rebrand after the 1970s, built from the remains of the Light and of other small anti-supernatural groups. It learned from the Light’s failures and became a movement that sounds reasonable. Members. Mostly newer Emsehurst residents, particularly people of Christian and other Abrahamic faiths together with secular atheists who share a distrust of what they call “fringe religious extremism.” In their view that covers both the Zingans and the Witches of Mephis. The two camps are held together by shared hostility, not shared belief. Public face. Deliberately faceless. Its online voice runs through one persona, and by the later books its posts have the cultural reach of the most influential political figures of the social-media age. Its dealings with witches. Some members buy enchanted items or fortifying spells from the very Witches the movement condemns. The 1970 raid. The most violent act in its history. It eliminated the Somerhalder presence in Emsehurst, whose seat has been vacant since, and killed two members of the Gilbert family. No human institution has formally acknowledged it. It is the wound at the centre of the supernatural community’s relationship with organised human hostility. The Basilica Sacrae Flammae The Sacred Flame Basilica calls itself a brother to the Coalition, with the same aims and different methods. The Coalition makes war with information, and the Basilica makes the other kind. Its members are mostly practising Catholics who treat the supernatural as a theological enemy instead of a social phenomenon. They hunt, and what they call purification ceremonies are executions. Leadership. None is known. It works like a leaderless militia, with regional cells and loud voices and nobody signing at the top. Look. Catholic imagery throughout: vestments, candles, Latin incantations and the vocabulary of crusade and inquisition. Its members are sincere believers, not costumes. The Church. The Catholic Church neither sanctions nor joins it. The Basilica found a theology already written and treated the Inquisition as a model, not a warning. Reach. At least six American cities. In Emsehurst it is a constant pressure that needs steady coordination between the Sekh, the Anu and their allies. Abilities Neither group has any supernatural ability from its beliefs. Members have the usual human weaknesses. Named individuals in both groups are left to the character material. Decided Emblems Emblem of the Human Coalition. Emblem of the Basilica of the Sacred Flame.

h: At a glance The five articles The 1964 addendum Who signed, by group In practice
x: Home / Earth / Emsehurst / Pandora’s Pact Pandora’s Pact An Agreement for the Protection of All Peoples Within the Bounds of Emsehurst. Signed in 1933, with a Lamiae addendum in 1964. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. At a glance Signed Emsehurst, 1933. Addendum 1964. Parties The Sekh, the Witches of Mephis, and a human witness. After 1964, also the Lamiae. Not parties The Anu, who are recognised as allies. Humans in general, who are protected by the Pact but did not sign. Court and army None. It is held by the word of those who signed. Length It does not expire and needs no renewal. The preamble says: “We agree to these terms not because we are alike, but because we must share what we cannot divide.” It was made, in its own words, “in necessity, in the middle of a broken world.” The five articles Article Terms I. Territory and conduct The Sekh hold the founding lands, the temple district and the Merveilles boundary. Their claim is the oldest and the Pact acknowledges it without granting it. The Witches hold their establishments, family homes and places of practice, and their contracts are their own business. Humans may live, work and move freely without harm or exploitation by any supernatural party. They are not property and not prey, and may not be fed on, bound or coerced without willing and informed consent. No party may wage war, hunt openly or use organised violence in the city against another party or against humans. Disputes go first to the named representatives. II. The Lamiae Not signatories in 1933. Their presence alone is not a breach. Feeding must be on willing participants of sound mind. Keeping bonded servants is the Lamiae’s own affair, provided nobody is taken by force from the general human population in and around Emsehurst. Organised predation on residents counts as aggression against every signatory. III. Grey areas and shared spaces Money Street, the University of Emsehurst, the Zingan Quarter and the SxSW districts are mixed territories. No party may use power, influence or numbers to dominate another’s members there. Grievances go through the representatives. The Anu hold the mountain and forest territories east of the Squannock, and no party may enter without their invitation. IV. Enforcement Each party answers for its own members, and the offending party’s representative is expected to answer for harm done. The consequence of breaking the Pact is that the peace ends. V. Duration and renewal The Pact holds as long as its signatories or their successors uphold it. If a party has no recognised representative in the city, its obligations go dormant, and resume if it returns. The 1964 addendum The signatories judged that the Lamiae of Emsehurst had acted in the spirit of the Pact and wished to formalise what had been an unwritten arrangement. The Lamiae became a full signatory with the same standing and duties as those of 1933. Their representative accepted Articles I to V as binding and took personal responsibility for his people’s conduct. The original terms were unchanged. Who signed, by group Group 1933 1964 The Sekh Two representatives Two representatives The Witches of Mephis One from each of the five founding families One from each of the five. The Somerhalder signer was killed in the 1970 raid, and the seat has been empty since The Lamiae Not a party Two representatives Human witnesses One, from the Bank of Emsehurst Two, from the Bank of Emsehurst and the Porter Trading Company Individual signers are left to the character material, not this almanac. Decided In practice The Pact’s protection covers every human in and around Emsehurst, not only those inside the city limits. Taking a person by force, and trafficking, breaks the Pact. Where it still happens, it is a breach, a tolerated abuse or a failure of enforcement. It is never something the agreement permits. Decided There is no supernatural court and no enforcing army. Everything rests on the Sekh and on the signers’ willingness to keep their word, and enforcement has been weaker in some years than in others. Decided Protection against humans being taken into Bediens status by force depends entirely on the Sekh being present and attentive. The Pact has no way to compel anyone. Its strength is that every party knows what comes after it. How the Pact treats voluntary contracts, coerced consent and permanent Servi bonds. The Lamiae run systems of human dependence that the Pact’s protection does not obviously allow Open

h: The creation, in short The gods The seven spirits of Mbòngómün Násítámün and the scarred moon Open questions
x: Home / Earth / Nẹránamün / The pantheon The pantheon Nyámün dreamed, and the gods are the dream’s children. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. The creation, in short In the beginning only Nyámün drifted in the void. Nyámün dreamed, and Time unfolded as a twin-faced being of mirrors. From Time came Chaos and Order, and from them the Death River, the Veil and the Serpent Guardian. Nyámün went on dreaming and shaped ocean, earth, stars, sun, flame and civilisation. Time’s turning brought wisdom, then Mbòngómün, ancestor of mortals, who was given seven animal spirits. The tellers close with a saying: “Time steps with two feet, yet leaves one path.” The gods Name Role Place in the family Nyámün The All-Creator Dreams the world. ‘Írukhmün Time, in two faces: ‘Írubámün (ebb: reflection, decay, wisdom, memory) and ‘Írábúkhmün (flow: momentum, life’s drive) First child of Nyámün. Their moons are Khùzú and Khùzí. ‘Ègúngumáyámün Order, weaver of balance and fate Younger twin, a child of both aspects of Time. ‘Ògùsémün Chaos, blacksmith of the gods Elder twin of Order. Kàtúngámün The Death River, which carries souls to the gates Elder child of Order and Chaos. Nèbémün The Veil of Souls, which separates the living world from the afterlife Younger child of Order and Chaos. Wạdíyèmün The Serpent Guardian of the crossings Child of Kàtúngámün and Nèbémün. Yémòmün Ocean Mother, supreme water goddess Second child of Nyámün. Wòtómün Earth Mother Third child of Nyámün. Násítámün Star goddess and steward of the unified moon Khùm Fourth child of Nyámün, made from stardust. Lòbárạmün The Sun King Fifth child of Nyámün. ‘Èn’zíngámün The Flame Queen and storm-flame goddess, maker of the Sekh Sixth child of Nyámün, elder twin of Chibíkunámün. Chibíkunámün Builder of civilisation, with thunder and lightning Seventh child of Nyámün, younger twin of ‘Èn’zíngámün. Thómítámün Wisdom and prophecy. Thómítámün’s sight shows the Mirror Trial. Child of Time and Násítámün. Nephew of the Flame Queen. Mbòngómün Ancestor of mortals, a demigod Child of Time and Wòtómün. Given seven animal spirits by Nyámün. ‘Anpésùmün Opener of Ways, who receives the shadow-soul at death Child of Chibíkunámün and Time. Hóshémün Sky King, god of wind Child of Násítámün and Lòbárạmün. Khósúmün Moon god and guardian of time’s cycles Child of Násítámün and Chibíkunámün. Símbìmün The Sea Spirit Child of Yémòmün and Wòtómün. Jèngùmün The River Spirit Made by Símbìmün. ‘Úbètímün Protector of warriors, Sunfire Child of ‘Èn’zíngámün and Lòbárạmün. Háshùmün Pleasure, joy and fertility Child of ‘Èn’zíngámün and Lòbárạmün. Anu pair-bonds are blessed in this name. Óshányemün, a child of Chibíkunámün and the Flame Queen, is planned but not yet developed. Placeholder The seven spirits of Mbòngómün Spirit Nok name Gift Link Gorilla ‘Èng’gímün Strength and family unity Sign 3 Canina (dog or wolf) Bùnumün Loyalty, pack leadership, spiritual guardianship The Anu’s heart patron Leopard Dùmeimün Stealth, shadow balance, mastery of twilight Shadow rites and warriors Lizard ‘Otukútámün Rebirth, survival, transformation Life cycles Chimpanzee Wòmün Cleverness, adaptability, innovation Lion Rómün Courage, ferocity, battle valour The Sekh’s heart patron Eagle Maizomün Vision, prophecy, dominion of the sky The Sekh’s solar guardian Násítámün and the scarred moon After the twin moons crashed together, the forces of ebb and flow still raged inside Khùm. Nyámün made Násítámün to be its steward: not the moon itself, but its shepherd, governor and soul. Sekh initiates may pray, “Násítámün, light my hunt. Hold the twin forces in your hands.” A prophecy warns: “When Khùm cracks, Násítámün will weep, and Daimùzónobu will tremble.” Open questions Mbòngómün is called both the eldest child and the youngest child of Time in the same line. Fix which. Open Yémòmün has no stated domain beyond the sea in the creation text, and several of the younger gods have only a one-line role. Open

h: Who is chosen Two paths Four phases The Four Trials Failure Blessing and naming After the fire
x: Home / Earth / The Sekh / Rebirth Rebirth and the Four Trials A human does not become a Sekh by wanting it. They die in fire, walk the Dream alone, and either return or dissolve. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. Who is chosen Becoming a Sekh is closer to sainthood than promotion. Most acolytes (Sèkhèt’mùna) serve the faith for their whole human lives, and Rebirth is a rare grace, not an expectation. When someone is chosen, the community holds a funeral on the scale of a saint’s canonisation, with celebration and mourning together. The human is honoured. Contact with family usually ends, because the bloodlust that follows makes proximity dangerous. Two paths Path A, from within the faith. Acolytes (Sèkhèt’mùna) are priests, ritual keepers, scholars and community servants. Most serve their whole human lives as devoted practitioners of Makésho. Those who are chosen already know the theology, the community and the 13 Dream-Tethered Signs. Path B, newcomers. A person may be met by a Sekh, recognised, chosen and brought through Rebirth with no earlier tie to Nẹránamün. They become a Sekh first, then learn Nọk, the theology and the shape of the world, and discover their own Dream-Tethered Sign. It is a disorienting road that Path A is not. Both groups meet at Moreau College ( Móró Khọzìyí ), where a Zingan devotee of twenty years may sit beside someone who was a civilian three months ago. See Schools . Four phases Phase Nok name What happens 1. The Burning Ng’nairèt’mün’éh The Initiator (‘Äkumukhèt) drinks from the initiate and feeds the initiate their own blood, a full exchange. They then trace ‘Èn’zíngámün’s sigil, Jaibüng’éh, on the initiate’s chest in the mingled blood. The Initiator’s divine blood and the sacred mark open the gate between the mortal world and the Daimùzónobu. The initiate enters the Dream as the rite takes hold, and the mortal body is consumed in flame. The soul walks alone from there. The Ikh’shímùyùnéh, the Flame-Blood Blade, was used only for the first attempts, the First Sekh’s own included, and never in a rite since. It belongs to Amadi alone. Decided 2. The Dream Thread Nígbamonatùn’éh The initiate walks the Four Trials alone. 3. The Divine Threshold Neirậpúwózím’éh If all four are passed, ‘Èn’zíngámün appears, flame-clad, and offers her blessing. 4. Awakening Ng’wásórèt’mün’éh The fire dies. The body is revealed, healed and marked. The Initiator speaks the new name. The Four Trials Trial Test Mnemonic and phrase Fail by Zúmánya, Breath Confront a moment of deepest despair and choose to live. Breathe. “I choose to live.” Surrendering to despair Ikhawaya, Flame Face your greatest fear and turn paralysis into action. Burn. “I move, even as fear burns within me.” Freezing or collapse Fùmányá, Mirror Witness your own potential for failure or corruption through Thómítámün’s sight. Acknowledge the shadow without denying it or giving in. Reflect. “I see my shadows. I choose my path.” Denial, or blind surrender Khaifùya, Dream Thread Navigate the Dream, fight only what must be fought, run when needed. Never fight everything, for pride blinds. Run. “I thread my path true.” Reckless fighting or fleeing Victory is a balance of breath, flame, self and instinct. Failure is an imbalance in the Dream. Failure A soul that fails is not punished or devoured. It dissolves into the Daimùzónobu, an untethered thread that is no longer a self. The Ghosthands of the House of Ash later find these threads and finish their dissolution, returning them to the fabric of the Dream. The Nok name for failed Rebirth is Kikíwàrï’khámé. This is not judgment. Blessing and naming Every successful initiate meets ‘Èn’zíngámün at the end of the Dream, and she gives the same blessing to all: “Child of my flame, you have walked the Dream and returned. Let your breath carry fire, your shadow walk true. Rise, new child of Sekh.” She named only the founding Zhèmuno clan herself. Everyone since is named by their Initiator or a senior clan member: “By the fire you carry and the thread you walk, I name you [Name]. Walk well among the Sekh, and let your thread burn bright.” Some acolytes prepare a name in advance, though tradition says to wait until after surviving. To awaken nameless is to walk unfinished. On rare occasions of destiny, the goddess whispers a name into the Dream once more. After the fire No shadow. Humans cast shadows because they walk beside the Daimùzónobu as a separate being. A Sekh internalises their shadow, the Khaifùya, during the last trial, so the body casts none. The Anu call the Sekh “Thread-runners.” The mark. The Khùnaimímaké appears on the skin, and the Khùzí shows as a living tattoo. Bloodlust. About a decade of danger to humans, longer for some. The Initiator and the clan become the Sekh’s whole world during it.

x: Home / Earth / Nẹránamün / Sacred arts Sacred arts and symbols Makésho is the craft of the sacred. It is earned through devotion, not inherited, so a lifelong human devotee can outdo an untrained Sekh. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. Makésho Makésho is open to Zingans and Sekh alike, through faith and dedicated study. It is not a birthright or a species ability. Decided Art What it is Practitioner Fùmamaké Sacred ritual tattooing. It uses a blend of the client’s own blood, which prevents the Sekh healing factor from rejecting the ink, and Fùmakégimé extract. It works on Sekh and humans alike. It was invented in the Ming era. Zingan sacred tattoo artists, who are its main practitioners Daigímíwaḳùn Dream ritual, veil-thinning and trance guidance with Dreamleaf. Daigímíyùn Nímawaḳùn Ritual healing, herb knowledge and thread-reading for illness. Nímayùn Daimùwaḳùn Prediction and counsel using the 13 Dream-Tethered Signs. Daimùyùn Ikhùwaḳùn Chant and blood rite in one: performance as ritual. Ikhùyùn, in the Ikhùkímùna tradition Sacred plants Plant What it is like Daigímí, Dreamleaf A rare silvery-green plant that grows near ruins, death-touched places, thin-veil sites and temples blessed by Násítámün. White-lilac flowers glow during Daimùzónobu moon phases. It burns with the scent of wet stone, sage and cedarwood, with a metallic note the Nok call “memory rain.” Used to sharpen spiritual sensitivity. Fùmakégimé, the Memory-Mark Herb A low shrub with deep blue-black berries that grows near places of long habitation, as though it remembers where people have lived. Tied to Wòtómün. It is not psychoactive. Its sacred property is permanence: marks made with it last. Symbols Symbol Meaning Jaibüng’éh ‘Èn’zíngámün’s sigil: a circle of flames with three tongues at the crown and one lower on the right. It is asymmetrical on purpose, because fire never burns evenly. It belongs to the goddess alone. An older temple form has thin, claw-like flames reaching out from a teardrop base. Both are sacred. Jaibütùw’éh The symbol of the faithful: the flame circle with an eye at its centre. “I am seen. I am of the flame.” Zingans and Sekh wear it alike, though the Sekh prefer not to be conspicuous. Khùnaimímaké The moon-star mark that emerges on a Sekh at Rebirth. Khùm is moon, naimí is star, maké is mark. The formal name is Khùnaimí makéní. Miyema bonyi The Anu’s together-bond mark: a crescent moon with a star and a dot above it, blessed by Háshùmün. Orders and clergy The Order of Shadows (Shùkízòròmùna, the ShadowKeepers) is the human order tied to the Anu. The Red Choir (the Choir of Red Dust, or Ikhùkímùna, the Flame Followers) is the ascetic Zingan sect: ritual dancers, oral keepers, blood-rite singers and temple guardians. Its devout monastic branch is the House of Ember . The Shùkí’Apésùmù (also Shùkapémù) are the human devotees of ’Anpésùmün as a faith group, the Anu-side parallel to the Zingans. The Order of Shadows is their organised order. An English name has not been chosen. Placeholder The House of Ash and its Ghosthands tend threads that failed Rebirth. Rites for the young Dunésí‘ibo, the Twin-Thread ritual. A child is placed on the Daimùkómbusubí mat, where Dreamleaf smoke drifts across their face and elders chant to Násítámün, Time or Nyámün. Observers stay silent while the Dream unfolds. The outcome is read as Feather (Shùnẹ) or Fang (N’zaikís). The weaves Píjai and Zídifézí are used in it. Kihódání‘obuwásóka, the awakening. A deeper rite that confirms a person’s true alignment when a quiz or earlier ritual is in doubt. Dúmùkwò, the thread tradition. See The thread tradition . Dreamleaf in daily life Outsiders see herbal incense and quiet temples. Inside, the same smoke is a doorway. Dreamleaf is the reason Nẹránamün temples keep gardens.

x: Home / Earth / The Nok / Schools Schools Nok education runs from play in the home to apprenticeships and capstone projects. A handful of named academies teach the faith and its fighters. Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. The Nok school path Stage Nok name Ages What it is like Infancy Kwóbizọnyí 0 to 13 months At home with parents or guardians. Primary Kwózonàyá 13 months to 8 years A Montessori-like system. Play, music, movement and hands-on exploration first. From age four, mixed-age groups so older children teach younger ones. Songs, weaving, cooking, nature knowledge, dance, tracking and cooperative problem-solving. Children are outdoors every day, rain or shine. The last year ends in a group camping trip with missions, and teachers watch from a safe distance. Elementary Kwọnázonàyá 9 to 14 Structured learning, social responsibility and critical thinking. In the long break students shadow a profession and join skill camps led by older mentors. At fourteen each completes a capstone passion project. Secondary Mètùzízonàyá 14 to 18 or 19 A four or five year programme with core courses and electives, developed through apprenticeships and camps. Postsecondary Khètuzízonàyá, Khọzíyí 18 or 19 and up University, or a training institute for specialty certificates, or work. Highly individual, with exams two or three times a year. Elementary, secondary and postsecondary details are still in development. Open The school year Two main terms, Kwómánèkh (first) and Kwímánèkh (last), with a summer term, Büyémánèkh, between them. Students attend five days of the six-day week. Kwómánèkh runs from ‘Anpémọnai 7 to Lòbárạdímọnai 12. Kwímánèkh runs from Nèbémọnai 1 to Kwọnákhạmọnai 24. Büyémánèkh is six weeks for school students and eight for university students. Older students use it for enrichment camps, capstones and apprenticeships. The long closing break, Kaiméshònítisei, covers Khèmọnai, so everyone is free for the sacred days. Every student takes a one-hour lunch and a mandatory one-hour siesta, in the dorms or a designated rest area. Festival breaks include a week for Tikhètùbẹsé, eight days around Zhawézónímís, and shorter breaks for the Sun, Harvest and Moon festivals. Named academies Each first campus was chosen for what the place offered, and many have a satellite elsewhere. School First campus Satellite Focus Yirimbo Zonémi Emsehurst, Old Temple Quarter, 1738 Lagos or Accra coastal hub, 1954 Cultural, spiritual and artistic preparation for children of the faith. Zhadín’kání Naibázonáyá, the Wild Heart Field School A Scottish highland glen, 1790 Cameroon rainforest annex, 1878 Survival and Fang-trial training outdoors. It teaches the full range from primary to secondary, has an ROTC division and feeds DMI. It is independent of the Mephis Consortium. Kizowufarù Zọnémí, Glasspoint Academy Lyon riverfront, 1885 Stockholm ambassadorial campus, 1927 Languages, diplomacy and covert statecraft. Daimushaifimí Military Institute (DMI) The Cimmerian Range, north of Emsehurst, 1912 None The elite martial and moral academy for the Anu. ‘Ikhukizowu Zoníyótí, Redvale Prep Johannesburg koppie, 1935 Montréal winter annex, 1962 Reform-minded preparation, with the Montréal campus a feeder for DMI. Zhufín’khái Naibázonáyá, River-Spirit Field School Upper Amazon, 1982 Survival campus in the Wild Heart family. Proposed Ki’àrù Zonémi, Sunrise Reef Academy Vanua Levu, Fiji, 1994 Liberal arts and diplomacy. Proposed Ngòdhaifimí Military Institute, Stormguard Institute Mindanao highlands, Philippines, 1975 A hardened sibling of DMI. Proposed The last three names are proposals and their Nok names are not final. Their stems borrow sound patterns from Tupi-Guarani, Fijian and Bisayan. Proposed Yirimbo Zonémi in more detail Motto: “Zhèmí dạkúmé shù wónírèt,” wisdom begins in wonder. The campus in Hurste, Emsehurst, blends Nubian curves for the Lower School (Yírímbo Zonémimètù) with Hausa geometry for the Upper School (Yírímbo Zonémikhètu), in earth-toned brick and limestone with lattice screens, green roofs, a campus farm, a ceremonial courtyard and a controlled flame basin. It is a private day and boarding school for the children of the Red Choir, Anu-aligned human families, Anu children who have not yet had their first shift, and humans drawn to the sacred liberal arts. It is not for awakened supernatural beings. Sekh aged nineteen or older enrol at Moreau College instead. It takes between 468 and 654 students, and it runs the whole Nok school ladder, so pupils range from small children to about 18 or 19. Proposed Daimushaifimí Military Institute “Dream Discipline.” Anu-aligned, for warcraft, rescue and supernatural leadership. Outsiders call it Dreamguard or Daimushai, and elders call it Sóróbusù Academy, “Standing Wolf Academy.” Students enter at nine to eleven after a rite of first light. Cadets move through the Daimúni phase (years one to five), then the Shadow Fang phase, with specialisations in healer, hunter, tactician, defender and scout. Moreau College Móró Khọzìyí is the post-secondary college where the faith’s two populations meet: Zingans who have studied for decades, and the newly Reborn who came to Rebirth by Path B. Top Yirimbo graduates receive scholarships. It is one of five such institutions in the world, in China, Brazil, Nigeria, France and Moreau itself. The witches’ schools The Conservatories of the Mephis Consortium are a separate system and are not part of the Nẹránamün school network. See The Mephis Consortium . h: At a glance How the Sekh began Two animal selves Shifting Abilities Weaknesses Marks of a Sekh Sekh blood Mates: Miyema Relations with other peoples The mate mark
x: Home / Earth / The Sekh The Sekh A Sekh in everyday dress. Concept image. Reborn hunters of flame. Each was a mortal who walked the Dream, died in fire, and came back stronger, wiser and carrying their shadow within. “What burns is alive. What endures is wise.” Lines without a tag are settled canon from the Earth reference documents. Tags mark anything less settled. Nok spellings follow the current reference documents. At a glance Name The Sekh, singular and plural. Pronounced “sek”, as in “seconds”. Native tongue Nọk, an agglutinative language. Place of origin Thamün’kebukhet, an ancient African empire and the cradle of Nẹránamün. Population About 100 to 150 worldwide. It has swelled to about 300 at moments of great threat. Every loss is felt. Age A Sekh stays the age they were at Rebirth. They cannot have children. Blood A special O-negative variant. Circulating blood decays at twice the human rate, and that decay powers most Sekh abilities. Initiating others Only a Sekh at least 100 years past their own Rebirth may Initiate a human. Eyes A Sekh keeps the natural eye colour they had before Rebirth, in every form. Oval pupils are the universal subtle tell. Gold irises appear only during mediation or ceremony, when ‘Èn’zíngámün moves through the medium, and in a brief pulse when the Khùzú awakens. Faith Nẹránamün, the faith of the Dream. How the Sekh began The Flame Queen, ‘Èn’zíngámün, watched mortals burn out before their fire had properly kindled. She resolved to reforge them: “stronger, wiser, carrying their shadows within.” Her first two attempts failed. The first was Chuki, an orphan child whose thread was too thin to hold, and only ash remained. The second was Kitwana, a proud warrior who did not survive the Mirror Trial. The third was Amadi, a soul that could hold the mirror steady without flinching. Amadi became the First Sekh. She was born about 309 BCE among the Kweizimuna of the Bamenda highlands, at the foot of Mt. Cameroon, and was reborn in 289 BCE at the age of twenty. Decided Today she is the head priestess of all Sekh, with the title ‘Ạmázingamün. Two animal selves Every Sekh has exactly two animal forms, one big cat and one bird of prey. They are not guardians or companions. They are the Sekh’s own soul in two registers. Harm to one is felt in the other. Spirit Meaning Made by Usual form Khùzí The born self. What the Sekh fundamentally is, revealed when Rebirth strips away everything constructed. ‘Írábùkh, flow, the waxing moon A big cat, present from Rebirth Khùzú The made self. What the Sekh becomes through trial, loss and relationship. ‘Írubá, ebb, the waning moon A bird of prey, awakened by a personal trial The Khùzú does not arrive on a schedule. About 100 years is only general guidance. When it wakes, a brief pulse of gold fires through the Sekh’s irises. Underneath, the two souls are Zhaní (the land-self or ego, expressed by Khùzí) and Zhané (the aerial self or id, expressed by Khùzú). A rare few Sekh invert the pattern: bird first, cat later. They arrive already elevated and spend their years earning groundedness. Big cats include cheetah, cougar, jaguar, leopard, lion, snow leopard, tiger and clouded leopard. Birds come from the hawks and eagles, owls, vultures and falcons. Shifting A Sekh must shift into one of their animal forms at least once a week. Suppressing either self causes real spiritual imbalance. The shift takes two seconds at most and is not painful. Humans nearby feel a wisp of warmth, then the animal is simply there. To another Sekh the outline briefly stops committing to one form, and the Rebirth fire shows as a heat-shimmer. Juniors look away when elders shift. It began as instinct and became a mark of respect. The animal form is larger and denser than any wild specimen of its species. Clothing does not shift by default. Objects the soul has claimed as its own travel with the Sekh. Elders can learn to extend the soul around clothing. Most Sekh keep spare clothes in cars and offices. Abilities Ability What it does Senses, strength and speed All senses are heightened. Strength is about ten times that of the strongest human under adrenaline. Shapeshifting Both animal forms, with a lean toward one of them. Whisper A voice that carries supernatural weight, usable in human form only. In encryption mode it makes Nọk unintelligible to non-Sekh ears. In compulsion mode it amplifies emotion and suggestion. To everyone nearby it sounds like a whisper, whatever the volume. Invisibility The body can still be smelled, touched and heard. It works especially well in daylight, when a Sekh has no shadow. Healing Surface wounds close in minutes and a severed limb regrows in days. Drugs and intoxicants wear off quickly. No ageing Rebirth rewrote the Sekh’s relationship with time. They are transformed, not artificially sustained. Spirit summoning In an emergency, near death, a Sekh’s animal spirit may appear on its own. Weaknesses Weakness Detail Sunlight Blessed by Lòbárạmün through ‘Èn’zíngámün, Sekh can walk in the sun, but long exposure makes them ill and dulls their senses to near-human levels. They are strongest at dusk and dawn. Large natural water Kàtúngámün, the Death River, flows through every large natural body of water. It does not recognise a Sekh, who has died but is not dead, and it saps their strength. Rain and baths are harmless, rivers weaken, and the open ocean can kill. Wạdíyèmün, the Serpent Guardian of the crossings, regards the Sekh with particular confusion, because they are anomalies in her domain. Lamiae blood Toxic to Sekh. Small amounts cause vomiting and unconsciousness, and large amounts kill. The only cure is a transfusion of Sekh blood. Lamiae saliva is dangerous too, from mild to fatal. Each people has made weapons from this mutual poison. Decapitation A Sekh cannot regenerate without the head reattached and blood to sustain it. Decapitation plus blood loss within the hour is fatal. Burnout A Sekh trapped in a loop of constant regeneration, with no way to refill their reserves, will exhaust their thread and die. Bloodlust Every newly Reborn Sekh (a Sámètù) endures about a decade of predatory hunger, called sainyíz hábai’èshöbüng, which makes being near humans genuinely dangerous. How long it lasts reflects the soul’s character as much as the body. A few struggle beyond the decade, and in extreme cases must be contained or put down. Marks of a Sekh They cast no shadow. See Rebirth . The Khùnaimímaké, the moon-star mark, emerges on the skin at Rebirth. The Khùzí appears with it as a living tattoo. Sekh blood Sekh blood is a weapon and a hazard to nearly everyone else. On Effect Anu An accelerant and an aphrodisiac, like amphetamine, with the same consequences. Lamiae Small amounts cause vomiting and unconsciousness. Large amounts are fatal. The cure is vomiting or bloodletting plus fresh human blood. Humans, Zingans included A steroid-like effect when it is not used in Rebirth, followed by a significant toll once the effects wear off. Mates: Miyema Thómítámün sees what each being needs and marks them so they may come together, or not. Háshùmün blesses and warms the bond. Pairing is always optional, and it works whatever species the other party is. Decided The mark. It sits on opposing sides of the neck on the two mates. The effects. If one mate is in danger, the other feels it. Across species. The Sekh partner carries the mark and the recognition. The other party can receive the bond once they naturally love. When it breaks. Rejection or death feels like dying slowly a second time. The mark bruises and fades over months or years. The Anu have their own expression of the same gift, with a bite at the base of the neck and a crescent-moon mark. See Rank, rites and bonds . Relations with other peoples People Relation The Anu Allies under the same pantheon. The Anu call the Sekh “Thread-runners.” Zingans The human faithful, including the Red Choir and the House of Ember. They practise Makésho, and many serve as acolytes. They are not bound to the Sekh. See Zingans . The Lamiae Older than the Sekh as a people and roughly equal in power. See The Lamiae . Their bloods are toxic to each other, and each has made weapons from it. The Lamiae signed the 1964 addendum to the Pact. The Witches of Mephis Opposed in principle, over souls that are trapped and tricked. The witches’ schools are a separate system. See The Witches of Mephis . Pandora’s Pact In practice the Sekh are the Pact’s enforcers. Its protection covers every human in and around Emsehurst. See Pandora’s Pact . The mate mark Mate mark of the Sekh.

Each sign has a Fang aspect and a Feather aspect, and two spirit paths: the Khùzí (born self) and the Khùzú (made self).
